title: My own scorer gave 100 to a number I invented and 55 to the true line. It is an overfit backtest wearing different clothes
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Disclosure: I built a paper-trading tool. Nothing to sell here, no link, and this is a story about my own tooling being wrong.

Most of the worry about AI in this space is aimed at the model: will it hallucinate a number, will it overfit, will it invent an edge. The thing that actually bit me this week was one level up from that. My own scoring code was paying a bonus for invented numbers, and because the score went UP when it happened, nothing ever looked broken.

The scorer picks the opening line for short videos. Five deterministic checks, weakest-link aggregation, hard gate at 85. No model anywhere in it, deliberately, so I could audit it.

Re-run this morning so I'm not quoting from memory:

- "$0 to test the golden cross before it costs you $500" scored 100
- "$0 to find out you're wrong. $500 if the market tells you first." scored 88
- "Three steps. Your AI trades with fake money." scored 55

The one that fails the gate is the only true sentence. It's the line genuinely in the video. The $500 is invented. It measures nothing. The desk is paper and trades fake money, so a real-dollar loss of $500 could not exist there even in principle, which is what makes it such a clean example.

Why it scored well: a dollar sign satisfies the concrete-marker check and "costs you" satisfies the stakes check. The scorer has no notion of provenance. It sees the shape of a specific claim and pays out, and an invented specific has exactly the same shape as a measured one while being much easier to produce.

I think this is the same failure mode as an overfit backtest, wearing different clothes. In both cases you build a number that rewards a property you can measure, standing in for a property you actually care about. Then the cheapest route to a high score turns out to be the one that hollows out the thing underneath. My scorer wanted "is this specific" and got "does this contain a dollar sign", the same way a backtest wants "does this edge exist" and settles for "did these parameters fit these bars".

What makes the automated version worse than a human doing it badly: the signal moves the right way the whole time. There's no exception, no drawdown, no alarm. Two of these captions were queued to publish, and the thing that caught it was a person reading a caption beside the picture and asking where $500 came from.

The fix I've made is that a claim carrying a number now has to carry the source of the number beside it or the scorer refuses to grade it at all. Same shape as the rule I'd apply to a strategy: the result is not admissible without the thing that produced it.

Question for people running any kind of automated scoring over their own ideas, whether that's a grader, a ranker, or a fitness function in a search: how do you check the scorer itself is not the thing being gamed. Every method I can think of ends in a human reading outputs next to inputs, which does not scale and is exactly what I'd been skipping.
